📍 Location: Makati City
🏢 Work Setup: Hybrid (4 days onsite, 1 day WFH)
Note: Fully onsite during the first 4 months for role transition.
🕗 Work Schedule: Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM

Are you an experienced technology leader with a strong background in software development, team management, and end-to-end product delivery?

We are looking for a Development Manager who will lead a multidisciplinary team of developers, business analysts, and QA engineers in driving software development, ensuring product quality, and maintaining the stability of live applications.

What You'll Do:
✔️ Lead, coach, and mentor a team of 16 professionals across .NET, Java, Web Development, Business Analysis, and QA.
 ✔️  Oversee the full Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), from planning and development to deployment and production support.
 ✔️  Manage Agile/Scrum activities, including sprint planning, backlog grooming, reviews, and retrospectives.
 ✔️  Ensure timely delivery of software projects while managing scope, resources, budgets, and risks.
 ✔️  Provide technical guidance on architecture, coding standards, software quality, and system integration.
 ✔️  Oversee production support, incident management, root-cause analysis, and SLA compliance.
 ✔️  Collaborate with Product Management, Operations, and business stakeholders.
 ✔️  Drive continuous improvement, team development, and process governance.

What We're Looking For:
✔️  Bachelor's Degree in Computer Science, IT, Engineering, or a related field.
 ✔️  At least 8 years of experience in software development.
 ✔️  At least 5 years of experience managing development teams of 5 or more members.
 ✔️  Hands-on experience in either .NET (C#, ASP.NET Core) or Java (Spring/Spring Boot), with working knowledge of the other.
 ✔️  Knowledge of modern web technologies such as JavaScript/TypeScript, HTML/CSS, React, or Angular.
 ✔️  Experience with relational databases and RESTful API development.
 ✔️  Strong experience in Agile/Scrum methodologies and project management tools such as Jira.
 ✔️  Background in production support, incident management, and QA practices.
 ✔️  Excellent leadership, communication, stakeholder management, and written English skills.

Nice to Have:
✔️  Experience with Azure, AWS, or GCP.
 ✔️  Knowledge of Docker, Kubernetes, and microservices.
 ✔️  PMP, CSM, SAFe, or ITIL certifications.
 ✔️  Experience managing hybrid/distributed teams and outsourced vendors.
 ✔️  Background in SaaS or product-based companies.

posts.text:
🧱 From Boxes to Building Blocks 🧱

I've worked in software engineering, program management, business development, consulting, and IT recruitment. Looking back, tech was easier to sort into boxes. 📦 Software, hardware, and infrastructure mostly sat in the customer's own data center. It wasn't easy, but it was clear who owned what.

Then things shifted. Microsoft's "Software Plus Services" push, and later hybrid cloud, let companies keep some things in house and hand others to outside providers. What I first saw as fragmentation, I now see as specialization. 


🔍 Specialization Is Showing Up Everywhere 🔍

We build differently now, too. Tools like React help developers organize big, complex apps. Splitting applications into services creates clearer boundaries, though the complexity just moves into the connections between the pieces. 


🎓 Certifications Got More Specific 🎓

Certifications followed the same path. Labels like Java, Oracle, and PeopleSoft once covered a lot of ground. Today, Microsoft has moved from MCSA, MCSD, and MCSE to role based certifications, and Kubernetes has separate credentials for administration, development, and security. Expertise is now described in smaller, more precise pieces. 


💡 Why Certifications Still Matter Now 💡

When job requirements get specific, employers want clearer evidence of what someone knows. In the Linux Foundation's 2025 State of Tech Talent survey, 71% of organizations said certifications are important when evaluating technical skills. Hands on experience and portfolios ranked even higher, so think of a certification as a solid starting point, not the whole story. 


🤝 A Win for Recruiters 🤝

From my recruiting days, I can tell you this helps recruiters, too. "Cloud engineer" only tells you so much. A relevant certification helps a recruiter ask sharper screening questions, compare candidates to what the hiring manager needs, and spot where more assessment is needed. Just know what each credential covers, since a foundational cert and an implementation focused cert aren't the same. It's about matching evidence to the work, not counting badges. 


🏁 Make Your Skills Easy to Recognize 🏁

A certification won't erase onboarding, since knowing a platform isn't the same as knowing a company's systems and team habits. Even AWS says there's "no true substitute for experience." Still, a relevant cert plus recent project work can shorten the road to contributing. 🚀 

In a tough job market, pick certifications that fit the work you want, pair them with real examples of what you've built or improved, and share that story with confidence. 🙌 

Certifications give employers a clearer starting point and a credible case that you can do the work. ✨

Think about where this started.

A decision made with more hope than certainty. A first client that felt like a miracle. The early months of figuring everything out as you went. The nights you were not sure it was going to work, followed by the mornings you showed up anyway.

You built something from nothing. That is not a small thing.

But here is what often gets lost in the middle of building.

The same determination that got the business started can become the thing that keeps it from growing. Because effort alone, sustained indefinitely, without a clear financial picture, creates a ceiling. You can work harder and harder and still not break through it. Not because something is wrong with you, but because the business has outgrown the systems it started with.

At some point, working more is not the answer. Working with better information is.

When you can see your real profit margin, you can price with confidence. When you understand your cash flow, you can plan instead of react. When your financial picture is clear, you can make decisions about growth, hiring, and investment that are based on reality rather than instinct.

posts.text:
AI can write the code.
A good software engineer still has to know whether it should ship.
I use AI every day as a frontend developer.
It helps me learn faster and improve the way I work.
The judgment about what reaches production still stays with me.
𝟭. 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿?
Subscriptions, API usage, infrastructure, maintenance, and review time belong in the same calculation as hiring.
The leverage is real.
A lower total cost still has to be proven.
𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲?
When I ship incorrect code, my team investigates and owns the fix.
When AI generates that code and I merge it, responsibility stays with:
• The person who reviewed it
• The team that released it
• The company that set the process
The provider supplies the tool.
Shipping remains a human decision.
𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲?
Over the next five years, companies will look for engineers who can frame a problem, choose an architecture, review generated code, protect security, and maintain what they ship.
𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜 𝗮𝗺 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴
• Fundamentals: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and the browser
• Problem framing and architecture
• Code review, debugging, and testing
• Security and product judgment
• Clear communication with design, product, and engineering
I plan to keep building these skills, use AI to learn faster, and understand every generated change before it reaches users.
I would like to hear your thoughts in the comments.
I respect your time, and I value every comment.

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
1. Has AI reduced your overall cost of software development?
2. Who should be accountable when AI-generated code causes a production issue?
3. Which skills are you focusing on to stay valuable over the next five years?

💬 𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. 😊 
There is a lot we can learn from each other. 👏

posts.text:
Recruiter: "So, do you know C?"

Me: "Yeah. I've been writing embedded C for about five years now."

Recruiter: "Great. And have you worked with React?"

Me: "..."

That little silence said a lot.

Look, I get it, recruiters juggle a hundred roles a day. But embedded hiring has this funny problem where the job and the interview sometimes feel like they're for two completely different roles.

The job is: bring up a board that's never booted before, chase a bug that shows up once a week and never the same way twice, make a CAN network behave, write a bootloader that must never brick a module.

The interview is: reverse a linked list on a whiteboard.

I'm not saying DSA doesn't matter. It does. But if you're hiring someone to debug real hardware, maybe ask them about the last board that didn't boot.

Embedded folks, what's the strangest question you've been asked in an interview for an embedded role?

posts.text:
We moved millions of records from MySQL to PostgreSQL while 700,000 people kept using the system. Nobody noticed. And data now loads 3x faster. 🚀

It was a nationwide training center platform in Iraq, used every day, so shutting it down for a weekend wasn’t an option.

We didn’t just copy the tables over. We redesigned the schema along the way. Same data, better structure, and that alone made reads 3x faster.

How we did it without downtime:
 - Tested our backups first, by actually restoring them
 - Kept MySQL running and added Postgres next to it
 - Sent every new write to both databases
 - Moved old data in small batches with checkpoints, so a failed batch just re-ran on its own
 - Compared both databases, then moved reads to Postgres bit by bit
 - Kept MySQL live until the very end, just in case

✅ Zero downtime
✅ Zero data lost
⚡ 3x faster reads

Biggest lesson for me: a good migration is boring. Lots of small steps you can undo, no big dramatic switch.

I’m a full-stack engineer in Dubai (Node.js, NestJS, React) and I’m open to new roles. Happy to chat if you’re hiring. 👋

My wellness chatbot used to repeat itself. Here’s how I rebuilt it.
Rowl AI is a mental wellness app I built and deployed. Version 1 worked, but Sera, its chatbot, had real problems: it ran on a retired model, it fetched the oldest messages instead of the newest, and refreshing the page wiped the conversation.
So I rebuilt the core for Rowl AI 2.0:
🧠 Three layers of memory: recent messages, a short long-term summary, and the user’s profile with their latest journal mood
🔁 A three-model failover chain on Groq, so one dead model no longer breaks the chat
🛟 A crisis safeguard on both client and server: a persistent support banner with one-tap helpline buttons, a calming grounding screen (breathing voice, soft tones, a haptic pulse), and an optional alert email to a trusted contact
👩‍⚕️ A doctor dashboard with an AI-written pre-session brief
🔐 Password recovery with a 6-digit OTP
☁️ Graceful fallback when the database is unreachable
The biggest lesson: the unglamorous parts matter most. Failure handling, safe defaults, and what happens when something breaks at 2am are what make an app feel trustworthy.
Rowl is a self-care tool, not a substitute for professional help.

The Miracle Morning:  Why Great Entrepreneurs Rush Slowly

The Reactive Trap

Most entrepreneurs start the day already behind. The phone lights up before the coffee does, an overnight email from a client, a cash-flow question from the bookkeeper, a team member who needs an answer now. Within minutes, we react instead of leading.

The Magic Morning

The most effective founders I work with protect what I call the "magic morning". The first 20 to 30 minutes of the day, before the world gets a vote. For many of them, the anchor is meditation.

Rush, Slowly

The Romans had a phrase for it. Festina lente, "make haste slowly." It sounds like a contradiction until you have run a business.  

MIT’s & MIG’s 
 
Old school, gain clarity on the Most Important Tasks and Most Important Goals that need to get done by simply jotting them down. Sure feels good checking them off, completing the day with that piece of paper in the trash can, ready for a fresh start tomorrow.

Power Down to Power Up

Think of your morning practice as powering down before the day powers up. Like a captain checking the instruments before leaving port, you are confirming your heading before the weather hits. 

You don't know what is coming to you today. A lost deal, a hiring crisis, an unexpected opportunity. You can decide who will be standing there when it arrives.

Then open the inbox. The day will still rush. You will just be the one setting the pace. 

#Pacing #Cadence #Clarity

posts.text:
He graduated from Princeton with perfect grades.

But his interviewer wasn’t impressed.

In the movie The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2012), Changez Khan interviews for a highly competitive financial analyst position at Underwood Samson.

He proudly explains that he’s never received a B and is about to graduate summa cum laude.

The interviewer, Jim Cross, barely reacts.

He’s already heard similar answers from several candidates that day.

Instead, Jim starts asking about Changez’s background, his financial struggles, and what motivates him.

Then comes the moment that changes the conversation.

Changez confidently tells him:

“Whether or not you hire me, Jim, I am going to win.”

The interviewer finally smiles.

What makes this scene interesting is the distinction between qualifications and motivation.

Academic achievements demonstrate discipline, intelligence, and consistency.

But they don’t necessarily reveal how someone responds to setbacks, handles uncertainty, or pursues difficult goals.

Great hiring decisions require understanding what candidates have accomplished and what drives them to accomplish more.

The strongest candidates bring more than impressive credentials.

They bring the determination to turn their potential into results.

#Leadership #Hiring #CareerDevelopment

posts.text:
261108 – Recently, a client complained to a coach, that the recruiter the client spoke to, was too abrasive. When I heard such a comment, I wondered to myself, “What is the purpose of the comment?”

Firstly, as job-seekers, our objective is to get the job. What we think of the recruiters, hiring managers, interviewers, or human recource personnels, is not important. Focus on what we need to do. We do not have to decide to turn down the offer, because we do not have the offer. We can withdraw our application, but have we assessed the opportunity thoroughly enough?

Secondly, when we watch the news, we focus on the news. We do not complain that the newscaster is being too negative. He/She is just reporting the news. We can choose not to watch the news when there is too much negativity. But for our job-hunt, we cannot afford to tune away, but only regulate ourselves accordingly.

In fact, we need to be conscious, are we emotionally affected by the news, or are we just unwilling to accept the truth? We can turn away temporarily. But to get to our goal, accepting the truth, and finding ways around it, is necessary.

Lastly, everything that we encounter is neutral. Positive or negative, is how we frame it. And in whatever that we do, focus on what we are trying to achieve, rather than being distracted by things around us. How we accept the things that we face, can help us to grow, developed our character, and make us better and stronger.

"Life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you react to it." The successful candidate who got the job, the colleague who got rewarded with a bonus and promotion, the pleasant service provider who got a superb review, the thriving business owner, they have their share of encounters with rude, nasty, abrasive, or even unreasonable individuals in their courses towards their goals. But they still thrive.

Do what is necessary, to get to where we want to be. There will be noises along the way. Tuning in to them, or shutting them off, is up to us. Our objective is to get to our goal, no matter what it takes.


=> we have an objective and a goal
=> there will be distractions around us
=> "Life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you react to it"
=> focus on our goal, and get to it, no matter what it takes

posts.text:
Every missed call is a patient who books with the next clinic. 📞 
So I built an AI receptionist for dental clinics, and it’s live. 😍 

It answers the phone in a natural voice, checks opening hours, and takes the booking request. The clinic’s staff then see the full transcript and a call summary in a private dashboard.
In the demo call, the caller asks for 12 AM. The assistant says the clinic is closed and offers 12 PM instead. The booking request lands on the schedule.
What’s under the hood:

→ Voice layer: Vapi (the call, speech and turn-taking)
→ Backend: Fastify + TypeScript, inputs validated with zod, webhook protected by a shared secret
→ Booking logic: opening hours, visit lengths and lead time in tested functions; Postgres advisory lock so two callers can’t take the same slot
→ Dashboard: Next.js 15 + React 19, signed-cookie login
→ Public demo reads a masked feed only: no phone numbers, no transcripts.

The clinic is fictional, but the build is real and you can try it yourself.
I’m a Senior Full Stack Engineer (React, Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, Python, Postgres, AWS) with 5+ years of experience. I’m open to remote contract roles, and I build AI assistants and web apps for small businesses.

If you’re hiring, or you run a clinic or service business that loses calls, send me a message.

posts.text:
99 cold emails in one inbox. 1 reply.

Watch the counter in the video.
It's one prospect's Monday morning.
(An illustration, but you've seen this inbox.)

99 emails say the same thing:
"Quick question about your growth."
Same tools. Same AI. Same template.

1 email says something else:
"Saw the hiring post for your new location. One idea for week one."

That's the one that got: "Good timing. Thursday?"

The difference isn't the writing.
It's knowing what just changed for them.

Doing that by hand takes hours a day.
So I built an AI system that does it for me:

1. Every morning it checks for signals
Job posts, funding rounds, new leaders, CRM switches.

2. AI checks each company against my ideal client
No fit, no email.

3. It writes one first line about what changed
Not "quick question". Not about me.

4. Replies land in my CRM with the signal attached
So I know why they answered before I open the email.

I still read every email before it goes out.
The system does the digging. I do the deciding.

Changing what I react to has moved my reply rates more than any copy tweak ever did.

The tools got cheaper.
Standing out didn't.

Comment SIGNAL and I'll show you how the system works.

posts.text:
Working in VA law enforcement gives us the privilege of serving a community that has already given so much.

Let’s face it, many of our Veterans have strong, Type A personalities. They’re direct, outspoken, independent, and not always interested in being told what to do. Some are dealing with pain, frustration, mental health challenges, or simply having a bad day. As VAP we’re going to be on the receiving end of that frustration.

Our job isn’t to win an argument. It’s to handle the situation professionally. Not every raised voice is a threat, not every disagreement is disrespect, and not every challenge to our authority requires a reaction.

When we allow our emotions to dictate our response, we risk escalating the situation, making the job harder for fellow officers and medical staff, and damaging the trust our community places in us. You can be firm without being disrespectful, assertive without being aggressive, and authoritative without being arrogant.

Professionalism doesn’t mean being a pushover. It means having the discipline, judgment, and emotional intelligence to know the difference between a genuine threat and someone who’s simply frustrated. We chose this profession, and with that comes a responsibility to uphold a higher standard, regardless of how others treat us.

Our Veterans don’t have to be easy to deal with to deserve dignity and professionalism.
Sometimes the greatest demonstration of authority is knowing when not to react.

Be firm. Be fair. Be accountable. Remember who we serve.

posts.text:
Junior devs, your LinkedIn headline is quietly costing you work.

"Full-stack web developer. HTML, CSS, JS, React, WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Python..."

You think that reads as versatile.
To the person hiring, it reads as "still figuring it out."

Here's the uncomfortable truth:
Nobody searches for a generalist.
They search for "fix my WooCommerce checkout."
"Move my site to Webflow CMS."
"Why is my Shopify store so slow?"

So pick one lane. Own it for 12 months.
Build three portfolio pieces that solve that exact problem.
Write about it here every single week.

It will feel like you're shrinking your options.
In reality, it's the moment people can finally find you.

Specialists get referred. Generalists get compared on price.

You can always widen later. Standing out on day one in a crowd of "I do everything" is the hard part.

If you had to pick ONE niche today, what would it be?

posts.text:
So, what does it actually take to become an AI Engineer in 2026?

I'm not sure. Competition is growing, and so is demand. But one thing is clear: #AIengineering skills are becoming increasingly valuable, even outside traditionally technical roles.

As I was learning AI engineering skills myself, I wanted to know what the market actually needs, rather than just follow online learning roadmaps.

So I analysed the latest 1,488 AI Engineer job postings (with comparison to 6,160 SWE roles) across #Switzerland, #Germany, the #Netherlands and other European markets (July–November 2026). ( P.S. This was made possible by Jobfish.ing, a platform we've been building to help #jobhunters apply for the right opportunities in the fastest way. )

Three questions I want to answer for myself:
1. What skills are employers looking for in AI Engineers?
2. How do these differ from traditional Software Engineers?
3. Which industries are hiring AI Engineers?

Some takeaways:

1. LLMs are becoming standard. Python (75%), LLMs (69%), AI Agents (51%) and RAG (49%) are the most frequently mentioned skills. Around 80% of roles focus on building AI applications, while only ~12% involve model training or research. In other words, think software engineering with an LLM stack.

2. AI Engineer and SWE roles have distinct skill profiles:

More common in AI roles: LLMs, RAG, Python, AI Agents and Machine Learning.
Shared by both: Architecture/system design, CI/CD, security and privacy.
More common in SWE roles: Java, React, SQL databases, clean code/design patterns and Agile/Scrum.

I've included the full analysis in the pictures.

Curious to hear: What AI engineering skills are you prioritising in 2026?

🚨 Hiring is broken, but the best startups are quietly fixing it.  

A few years ago, recruiters would CTRL+F for keywords—"React, 5+ YOE, AWS"—and call it a day. Now? The best teams don’t care about your resume bullets. They care about what you’ve *built* and how you solve real problems.  

Forward-deployed engineers, proof-of-work projects, and take-home challenges that mirror actual work are replacing leetcode hazing. The shift is simple: **Can you do the job, not just interview for it?**  

The data shows it—high-growth startups are 3x more likely to prioritize shipped work over pedigree. And honestly? It’s about time.  

How’s hiring changed for you lately? Seeing more practical assessments or still stuck in the resume black hole?

Our entire stack is built in a modern, unified TypeScript ecosystem—no context-switching between backend languages. You will work directly on serverless architecture, AI extraction pipelines, database integrity, and webhook-driven billing systems.

What You’ll Do
Maintain & Scale the Core App: Own full-stack development across our Next.js App Router, React Server/Client Components, and Node.js serverless runtimes.

Refine AI Extraction Pipelines: Maintain and optimize document parsing workflows using LLM APIs (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI) and local PDF text processors (unpdf), ensuring strict balance reconciliation and zero data leakage.

posts.text:
A REQUEST TO RECRUITERS & HR PROFESSIONALS 🙏

Dear Recruiters, HR Professionals and Hiring Managers,

Please understand the feelings of job seekers.

When you publish a job vacancy on LinkedIn, many people react, comment and show interest. Some candidates politely comment, "Please share your resume."

Job seekers trust your words, prepare their CVs and send their resumes with hope of getting an opportunity.

But unfortunately, after receiving the resume, many recruiters don't respond. No interview call, no rejection message, not even a simple update.

Please remember:

- A job seeker's time is valuable.
- Every resume represents someone's hope and hard work.
- Not every candidate will be selected, and that's absolutely fine.
- But a simple response can make a big difference.
- If a candidate is not suitable, please communicate it politely.

You don't have to give everyone a job, but you can give everyone a response.

Behind every resume, there is a person waiting for an opportunity, someone working hard to support their family and build a better future.

Respect job seekers. Respect their time. Respect their hopes.

Let's make LinkedIn a platform for genuine opportunities, not just collecting resumes.

posts.text:
I built my own Vercel from scratch. 🚀
You sign in with GitHub, pick a Vite/React repo, and the platform builds it in an isolated AWS Fargate container. Build logs stream live to your browser, and the site goes live at <slug>.yourdomain.com. A git push redeploys it automatically.
Under the hood it’s 10 backend services in a TypeScript monorepo, using Express, Postgres, Redis, BullMQ, Kafka, ClickHouse, S3 and Socket.IO. These were the parts that taught me the most:
🔒 One active build per user. A Redis lock stores the owning deployment ID and is released with a Lua compare-and-delete. A late cancel can never free a lock that now belongs to someone else. Postgres compare-and-set updates mean a cancelled deploy can never flip back to “ready”.
📡 Live logs with no gaps or duplicates. Container → Kafka → two consumer groups. One fans out over Socket.IO and the other persists to ClickHouse. Every event carries a per-deployment sequence number. The browser subscribes first, then fetches history, then merges by sequence.
🔑 Auth that assumes tokens get stolen. Refresh tokens rotate on every use. If an old one is replayed, an atomic Lua script detects it and revokes the whole session.
🛡️ Safer builds. User code runs with a minimal environment, so platform secrets are never visible to it. Secrets are redacted from every log line, including URL-encoded and base64 forms.
The biggest lesson: the happy path is the easy part. The real design work is in cancellations, crashes, retries, duplicate webhooks and Kafka outages.
I’m a final-year B.Tech student looking for Software Engineer roles in India. If you’re hiring, or just want to talk distributed systems, I’d love to connect.

New here, or been reading all week? One post about working with me — then back to the useful stuff.

I am Muhammad Hamad, a Full Stack Developer and AI Engineer with 8 years of experience, working remotely with clients and teams worldwide.

Most good projects I have seen do not start with "build us an AI system". They start with one workflow that wastes a team's week.

So here is how working with me usually starts:

1. You describe the workflow that wastes your team's time — leads, data entry, follow-ups, documents, support.
2. I tell you honestly whether AI, automation, or simple software is the right fix — including when the answer is "do not build anything yet".
3. We start narrow: one task, clear rules, a human checking the important steps. Then we expand only if it works.

What I build around that first step: workflow automation, AI features and agents with rules and limits you control, and the software around them — SaaS platforms, dashboards, and internal tools.

My stack: Python, TypeScript, React, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI — plus OpenAI and Claude APIs, LangChain, and retrieval systems.

Two ways to start a conversation:
- Businesses: message me the workflow. I will reply with the first step I would take.
- Recruiters and hiring managers: message me the role. My portfolio and experience are at hamadshafiq.com.

No pressure, no pitch beyond this post. Tomorrow we go back to teaching.

Which workflow would you bring to that first conversation?

posts.text:
One bug in our SkilledCoder test let anyone take over any user’s account.

It was one of 6 bugs we planted in a realistic login system. Last night I ran a full walkthrough of the test to see exactly what a candidate sees.

The candidate gets an AI assistant, just like at work. But the AI won’t find the bug for you. You have to find it, tell the AI exactly what to fix, and explain why it broke.

My report: 86 out of 100, 5 of 6 bugs fixed. It scored my efficiency 43 and told me to give the AI one clear, specific instruction up front.

That’s the skill now. AI can write the fix. The engineer has to know what’s wrong and what the fix should be.

Last week 48 engineers signed up and 36 took a test. Most ran out of the 60 minute clock.

If you hire engineers, this is the skill worth testing for.

Engineers, suggest our next challenge. Reply with stack + bug, like:
Go: two workers pick up the same job
Node: users still see old data after an update
React: form submits twice on a double click

The most requested one gets built next.

Try it free: skilledcoder.ai/practice

Happy Diwali  🪔

Here is the October 2026 update for the Hacker News "Who's Hiring" index.

545 job postings in October, up from 539 in September and down from 796 in October last year. Median pay went down to $185k, from $195k.

• July, August, September and October were the four quietest months in over 12 years. There have been 6,400 postings so far this year, 12% fewer than the same months of 2025.
• In 11 of the previous 14 years, October had more postings than September. This year it had 6 more.
• Remote roles paid a median of $170k and onsite roles $219k. Remote has paid less than onsite every month since February. From October 2025 to January 2026 remote paid more. Half of all posted salaries were between $165k and $220k.
• TypeScript, Python and React were the most-requested skills. About 1 in 5 postings asked for an AI or machine learning skill, about the same as September. Claude Code was the AI coding tool named most often, as it has been every month since March.
• Remote was 48% of roles, hybrid 24% and onsite 28%. Remote has been between 45% and 53% every month for the past year. UK roles went from 33 to 58, the most since June.
• Engineering was 61% of postings. In October 2024 it was 74%. Data and ML went from 12% to 15% over the same two years.
The November update will be out in early December.

- Minimum 4 years of experience as a Piping Engineer in an Engineering Consultant company.
- Experienced in Onshore and Offshore Oil & Gas projects.
- Bachelor's Degree (S1) in Mechanical Engineering, Piping Engineering, Materials and Metallurgical Engineering, or related disciplines.

2. INSTRUMENT ENGINEER
Requirements:
- Minimum 4 years of experience as an Instrument Engineer in an Engineering Consultant company.
- Experienced in Onshore and Offshore Oil & Gas projects.
- Bachelor's Degree (S1) in Instrumentation Engineering, Physics Engineering, Electrical Engineering, or related disciplines.

3. PROCESS ENGINEER
Requirements:
- Minimum 4 years of experience as a Process Engineer in an Engineering Consultant company.
- Experienced in Onshore and Offshore Oil & Gas projects.
- Bachelor's Degree (S1) in Chemical Engineering or related disciplines.

GENERAL REQUIREMENTS
- Indonesian citizens only (WNI).
- Familiar with applicable engineering standards, codes, and international standards relevant to the respective engineering disciplines.
- Able to work independently and collaboratively in a multidisciplinary team.
- Strong problem-solving skills and able to work under pressure and meet deadlines.
